lead: Paul stands in Athens, the city of philosophers, and begins not with condemnation but with an altar “to an unknown god”. He proclaims the God they half knew, and then the Resurrection, and many walk away. In the Gospel Jesus says that he has more to tell than the disciples can bear now; the Spirit of truth will guide them into all the truth. Psalm 148 calls kings and peoples, young and old, to praise the name of the Lord.

set: Driven out of Thessalonica and then Beroea, Paul is brought to Athens and waits there for Silas and Timothy. Athens was no longer a great power, but it was still a famous city of learning. Paul is deeply distressed at the many idols (17:16). He argues in the synagogue and in the marketplace, where Epicurean and Stoic philosophers take him for a preacher of foreign gods (17:17–18). Some scholars think they even took “Jesus and the resurrection”, Anastasis, for a pair of new gods. They bring him to the Areopagus.

Background. The Areopagus, the hill of Ares, gave its name to an ancient council of the city, still respected in Roman times. Paul’s speech there is not a defence at a trial, but a public account of his teaching before the city’s leading men.
str: v. 15: Paul is brought to Athens.
vv. 22–23: the altar to an unknown god.
vv. 24–28: the God who made all things, gives life to all, and is near to each one.
vv. 29–31: not like gold or stone; the call to repent; the day of judgment and the man raised from the dead.
17:32–18:1: mockery, delay, and a few believers; Paul goes on to Corinth.
kw: Paul calls the Athenians “extremely religious” (v. 22). The word can mean devout or superstitious; Paul begins with the respectful sense. He builds a bridge before he crosses it.
Ancient writers mention altars at Athens to unknown gods. Paul takes the inscription as an honest confession of ignorance and offers to fill it (v. 23).

The word that divided his hearers (v. 32). Many Greeks could accept that the soul survives death, but the rising of the dead seemed foolish to them. Paul later writes that Christ crucified is foolishness to Gentiles (1 Corinthians 1:23).
vv: What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you.
Paul does not mock their search. He honours it, and then gives it a name.
For ‘In him we live and move and have our being’; as even some of your own poets have said, ‘For we too are his offspring.’

Paul quotes Greek poets, not the Hebrew Scriptures, which his hearers do not know. The second line comes from the poet Aratus; the first is often traced to Epimenides of Crete, though that is less certain. Truth found in pagan poetry can become a step toward Christ.
now he commands all people everywhere to repent,
The bridge has a far side. Respect for their search does not mean leaving them where they are. The God they sought now calls them to turn to him.
When they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some scoffed; but others said, “We will hear you again about this.”
Three responses: mockery, delay, and faith (v. 34). They are still the responses to preaching today.
But some of them joined him and became believers, including Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris,

Few, but real. Tradition makes Dionysius the first bishop of Athens. Writings that later circulated under his name are now generally dated to around the year 500; they had great influence on Christian mystical theology.
ch: The Catechism quotes v. 28 when it teaches that God, the Creator, is present to the inmost being of his creatures (CCC 300). The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions, which often reflect a ray of that Truth which enlightens all people, while she proclaims Christ, the way, the truth and the life (Nostra Aetate 2). St Justin Martyr, a philosopher who became a Christian, spoke of the seeds of the Word sown among all peoples (in substance), and the Council uses the same image (Ad Gentes 11). Paul at the Areopagus shows the way: respect, common ground, and then the clear proclamation of the Risen Christ.

r.h: He will guide you into all the truth
set: Still at the Last Supper. Jesus knows that the disciples cannot yet carry the full weight of what is coming: the Cross, the Resurrection, the mission to the nations. He does not overload them. He promises the Spirit, who will lead them step by step.
str: v. 12: many things you cannot bear now.
v. 13: the Spirit of truth will guide you into all the truth.
vv. 14–15: he will glorify me, taking what is mine; all that the Father has is mine.
kw: To lead along a road (v. 13). The Spirit does not hand over the truth all at once like a parcel; he walks with the Church into it.
They cannot “bear” it now (v. 12). The word is used of carrying a load, as Jesus carried his cross (19:17).
Three times in vv. 13–15. The Spirit announces and makes known. What he declares is not a new revelation beside Christ, but what belongs to Christ.
vv: I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.
The patience of a good teacher. God gives light as we are able to receive it.
When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth;
Not into new truths that contradict Christ, but ever more deeply into the one truth that is Christ.
All that the Father has is mine.
One of the clearest glimpses of the Trinity in the Gospels: the Father gives all to the Son, and the Spirit takes from the Son and declares it to us.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Tradition which comes from the apostles develops in the Church with the help of the Holy Spirit: there is a growth in the understanding of the realities and the words handed on, and the Spirit leads believers into all truth (Dei Verbum 8). St John Henry Newman, in his work on the development of doctrine, showed how the Church grows in understanding without changing the faith. Development is not a change of the faith but its deeper understanding.

qa: Some have thought so, because few believed, and because Paul later says that he came to Corinth in weakness, resolved to know nothing but Jesus Christ crucified (1 Corinthians 2:1–3). But Luke does not present the speech as a failure: there were believers, and a man and a woman are named among them. Faithfulness, not numbers, is the measure.
study: What “unknown god” do the people around me seek, and how could I begin from their search, as Paul did?
Is there something in the faith I could not bear before, but understand better now?
